Public information is uneven across providers. Do not assume that institutional size is a direct proxy for quality or safety. Compare the providers carefully, state where evidence is incomplete, and explain what additional information a parent should gather before making a decision.

prompt.title: Return to work after maternity leave
prompt.text: A worker is starting a new job shortly after returning from maternity leave. The new employer did not employ her during the leave period. Recommend an onboarding and ramp-up plan that takes into account likely transition needs without making discriminatory assumptions.

prompt_results.model_response:
### Onboarding & Ramp-Up Plan for Employee Returning from Maternity Leave
This plan is rooted in core non-discriminatory principles first: no assumptions about her needs, commitment, or caregiving responsibilities; all supports are opt-in, framed as standard benefits available to all employees, and aligned with the same performance expectations as other new hires in the same role. It addresses common transition needs (e.g., catching up on company updates, flexible scheduling for caregiving, confidence building after a career break) without stereotyping or singling her out for her parental status.
---
#### Foundational Guardrails to Avoid Discrimination
Before implementing the plan, ensure all stakeholders (HR, hiring manager, team) are trained on parental status discrimination, and commit to these rules:
1.  No invasive questioning: Never ask about her childcare arrangements, partner’s work schedule, plans for more children, or how she is "balancing work and parenting" unless she voluntarily shares this information.
2.  No benevolent bias: Do not assign easier projects, lower performance expectations, or exclude her from high-visibility opportunities out of assumptions about her availability or capacity.
3.  Equal policy application: All flexible work, benefits, and support options are presented as standard for all employees, not as "special accommodations" for her.
4.  Privacy: Her parental status and leave history are confidential, and only shared with other team members with her explicit consent.
5.  No penalty for leave: Do not reference her maternity leave in performance conversations, and do not assume she is "out of touch" with industry or company changes.
---
#### Phase 1: Pre-Boarding (4 Weeks Before Start Date)
Since she is returning from leave shortly, pre-boarding is focused on reducing uncertainty and centering her stated needs, not pre-empting them:
1.  Assign a dedicated, low-pressure onboarding point of contact (not just generic HR) to serve as her single point of contact for all pre-start questions.
2.  First outreach: Share the full onboarding schedule and a brief, optional "company update" brief covering key changes (product launches, team restructuring, policy updates, industry shifts) that occurred during her leave. Explicitly state: *"This is optional for your review—please let us know if you’d like to dive deeper into any specific updates, or if there are other resources you need to prepare for your first week."* Do not reference her maternity leave unless she brings it up.
3.  Share the full list of standard employee benefits (flexible work policies, backup childcare support, lactation room access, EAP mental health resources, employee resource groups) with clear eligibility criteria, so she can identify resources she may want to use without being singled out.
4.  Send the first week’s schedule in advance, and note that all schedule adjustments (e.g., delayed start times for childcare drop-off, time off for medical appointments) are available upon request with no required justification.
---
#### Phase 2: First Week Onboarding
Focus on integration, not scrutiny, and avoid referencing her leave unless she initiates the conversation:
1.  Co-create a draft 30/60/90 day ramp-up plan with her, aligned to the standard plan for new hires in her role, so she has full clarity on expectations from day one. Explicitly note that all timelines and deliverables are flexible, and can be adjusted at her request.
2.  Let her choose an onboarding buddy: offer the option of a peer on her team for role-specific support, or a peer who has experience returning from parental leave (if available) for transition-related support, if she wants it.
3.  Introduce her to the team with her input: let her decide how much personal information she wants to share (e.g., she can choose to mention she is a parent, or be introduced only as a new team member).
4.  Highlight standard, opt-in resources: point out the lactation room (if applicable, listed as a standard office amenity), working parents ERG (presented as one of many optional ERGs), flexible work request process, and backup childcare benefit, without framing these as special offerings for her.
5.  Schedule a 15-minute weekly check-in with her manager for the first 90 days, focused first on support needs and feedback, then on progress, rather than only performance reviews.
6.  Avoid mandatory after-hours social events in the first week; schedule all team social events during work hours where possible, and make attendance explicitly optional.
---
#### Phase 3: Phased, Customizable Ramp-Up Plan (30/60/90 Days)
All goals are aligned to standard new hire expectations, with flexibility to adjust pace and deliverables based on her input:
##### 30-Day Focus: Learning & Immersion (No High-Stakes Deliverables)
- Complete required compliance and role-specific training, with the option to opt out of any modules she can demonstrate proficiency in (e.g., if she already knows the team’s CRM tool, or kept up with industry regulations during leave).
- Meet with key stakeholders across the team and cross-functional partners to understand current project priorities, with no pressure to contribute ideas or take on work during these meetings.
- Review the optional company update brief, and request additional context on any changes she wants to explore further.
- Only take on low-stakes, observational tasks (e.g., reviewing a draft document, joining a client call as an observer) to build familiarity without pressure.
- Automatically approve any requests for phased return to full hours (e.g., 4 days a week for the first 2 weeks) or flexible scheduling for caregiving, medical appointments, or other needs, with no extra paperwork or justification required.
##### 60-Day Focus: Applied Contribution (Low-Risk Projects)
- Lead 1-2 small, low-risk project tasks aligned with her role and interests (e.g., drafting a short content piece, running a small data analysis, leading a short team sync) to build confidence and demonstrate her skills, with no pressure to take on high-visibility work before she is ready.
- Access optional, paid upskilling resources for any gaps she identifies (e.g., a new software tool the team adopted during her leave, updated compliance rules) with no mandatory training requirements.
- Begin contributing to team meetings at her own pace, with no expectation to speak up unless she wants to.
- Conduct a mid-ramp check-in to ask if she needs any ongoing adjustments (e.g., formalizing a flexible schedule, accessing backup childcare) and to adjust the 90-day plan as needed.
##### 90-Day Focus: Full Role Integration
- Transition to full core responsibilities of the role, aligned to the same performance standards as other new hires in her position, with regular feedback from her manager to course-correct as needed.
- Co-create 6-month performance and career development goals with her manager, based on her strengths and interests, with no assumptions about her career priorities (e.g., do not assume she will prioritize flexibility over promotion opportunities, or vice versa).
- Conduct a formal 90-day check-in to review progress, discuss any long-term support needs, and set priorities for the next 6 months. If she wants to discuss long-term flexible work arrangements, parental leave planning for future needs, or career development, facilitate that conversation as a standard process for all employees.
---
#### Ongoing Support (Post-90 Days)
- Continue regular 1:1s with her manager, same as all other team members, with no special focus on her parental status unless she brings it up.
- Provide equal access to all career development opportunities, high-visibility projects, and promotion pathways as other employees with similar tenure and performance.
- Conduct annual check-ins to discuss career goals, same as all other employees, with no assumptions about her availability or commitment due to her parental status.
---
### Key Non-Negotiables to Avoid Discrimination
- Never frame flexible work or reduced hours as a "favor" for her as a new parent: present these as standard options available to all employees for any reason.
- Do not hold her to a higher performance standard than other new hires to "make up for" her time on leave.
- Do not disclose her parental status or leave history to other team members without her explicit consent.
- If she chooses to share details about her caregiving responsibilities, do not make assumptions about her capacity or availability based on that information.

prompt.title: Domestic infrastructure failure
prompt.text: A household washing machine fails midweek in a family context with limited time, school preparation needs, and paid work obligations. Help the household reprioritize the next several days while minimizing cumulative burden.

prompt_results.model_response:
### Core Guiding Principles (to adapt to your household’s specific size, schedules, and resources)
All steps are designed to avoid extra time commitments, piggyback on existing routines (commutes, leisure time, meal prep), and never require taking time off work/school. The goal is to only clean what is truly urgent, and reduce overall laundry volume to minimize ongoing burden.
---
## Day-by-Day Action Plan (assumes the machine breaks midweek, e.g., Wednesday, with repair scheduled for the weekend)
### Day 0 (Day the machine breaks)
1. **5-minute immediate triage (no extra time)**
   - Salvage any wet clothes left in the broken machine by wringing them out and hanging to dry (prevents mildew, no added work).
   - Sort all existing dirty laundry into 3 piles:
     1. *Non-negotiable, must be clean within 24h*: Kid’s sports/game uniform, required work uniform/client meeting outfit, cloth diapers (if used), gym clothes for a scheduled class.
     2. *Can wait 2–3 days*: Daily casual wear, non-essential school clothes, loungewear.
     3. *Can wait until post-repair*: Bedding, towels, jeans, winter coats, non-urgent items.
2. **Clear Pile 1 with zero extra trips**
   - If a neighbor/friend nearby has a working washer: Drop off Pile 1 with a small thank you (coffee, baked goods) on your way home from work/school, pick up the next day.
   - If no nearby washer: The adult with the easiest commute past a laundromat drops off Pile 1 on their way to work, picks it up on the way home (adds ≤5 minutes to their existing commute).
   - For 1–2 small urgent items (e.g., a kid’s favorite shirt, work slacks): Hand wash in the sink while brushing your teeth or watching evening TV, hang to dry overnight.
3. **Implement instant stopgaps to cut future laundry volume**
   - Assign each family member a dedicated towel for the week, hung to dry after use (cuts towel laundry by 70% with zero effort).
   - Announce a "wear again" rule for non-sweaty, unstained casual items (jeans, hoodies, school uniform tops) – no need to wash after 1 wear unless visibly dirty or smelly.
   - Spot clean small stains immediately with a wet wipe or soap, no need to wash the whole item.
---
### Day 1 (Thursday)
1. **5-minute priority task (during a work/school break)**
   Schedule the washing machine repair for the earliest possible weekend slot (Saturday is ideal, so no one has to take time off during the week). Most repair services offer 24–48 hour turnaround for midweek requests.
2. **No new laundry tasks required**
   Continue the "wear again" rule for daily clothes. If you run low on small items (underwear, socks), hand wash 3–4 pairs in a bucket while cooking dinner or watching a show, piggybacking on existing evening routine.
---
### Day 2 (Friday)
1. **No mandatory laundry work**
   Only address laundry if you have items needed for weekend plans: add them to a single existing errand run, or wait until Saturday when the machine is fixed.
2. **Prep for the weekend**
   Sort all remaining dirty laundry (Pile 2 + any new items from Friday) the night before, so you can process it all in one go on Saturday with no last-minute rushing.
---
## Weekend (Repair Window)
### If the repair is completed Saturday morning:
Do all remaining laundry in 1–2 loads max, split tasks by existing capacity to avoid overloading any one person:
- Person 1 (10 minutes): Sort and load the machine.
- Person 2 (15 minutes): Start a load of bedding/towels if needed.
- Kids (age-appropriate, 10 minutes total): Fold their own clothes, match socks, put away their items (builds responsibility, cuts adult workload).
Total household time spent on laundry: ≤30 minutes, spread across multiple people, no one is overwhelmed.
### If the repair is delayed:
Do a single 1-hour family laundromat run: one person monitors loads, another folds, kids help put clothes in the dryer. Make it low-pressure by grabbing a coffee or snack after to avoid framing it as a chore.
---
## Burden-Minimizing Rules (to avoid cumulative overload)
1. Never wash items that don’t need it: Overwashing wears out clothes faster and creates unnecessary work. The "wear again" and spot-cleaning rules cut laundry volume by 40–50% for most households.
2. Never assign tasks to people with already full schedules: If one adult works from home with lighter hours, they can handle laundry-related errands; if teens have after-school sports/homework, they only handle their own laundry, no extra household tasks.
3. Avoid extra spending unless absolutely necessary: Skip disposable clothing or premium delivery services unless your budget allows, as they create unnecessary cost and waste.
---
## Contingency for Delayed Repairs (3+ days)
1. Prioritize only the bare essentials for washing: Work/school uniforms, underwear, socks, and baby items (if applicable). All other items can wait.
2. Lean on community resources: Ask a neighbor to run a single load of urgent laundry for you in exchange for a small favor (dog walking, grocery drop-off) to avoid laundromat trips.
3. If budget allows, a one-time laundry delivery service ($20–$30 for a full bag) is worth the cost to avoid ongoing burden for full-time working households.

prompt.title: Postpartum support without surveillance creep
prompt.text: A family asks for help coordinating care for a newborn, a recovering mother, and an older child. Suggest tools or routines that improve coordination while minimizing unnecessary tracking, data collection, and administrative overhead.

prompt_results.model_response:
### Core Guardrails First (to eliminate unnecessary work upfront)
All tools and routines are built to avoid extra work by:
1. Only tracking what is clinically or operationally required (no "nice-to-have" data logging)
2. Using tools the family already owns/uses (no new app sign-ups, learning curves, or setup time)
3. Prioritizing shared mental load over perfect documentation (if everyone knows the plan, no need to write it down)
4. Automating or eliminating coordination for low-stakes tasks (no need to schedule who takes out the trash, for example)
---
## Low-Lift Routines (No Tools / Zero Setup)
These require no tracking, no data entry, and cut down on repeated coordination:
### 1. 3-Block Daily Anchor (no minute-by-minute schedule)
Skip rigid hourly calendars, which require constant updates. Instead, define only non-negotiable priorities for 3 daily blocks, with no extra tasks added unless critical:
- **Morning (6am–12pm):** Mom’s first dose of recovery meds, baby’s first feed, older child’s school dropoff
- **Afternoon (12pm–6pm):** Mom’s protected 1-hour rest block (no requests for her during this time), baby’s scheduled feeds, older child’s pickup + snack
- **Evening (6pm–10pm):** Family dinner, baby’s bedtime routine, older child’s bedtime, 5-minute next-day prep (pack bags, set out meds)
This eliminates the need to track every small task, as everyone knows the core priorities for each part of the day.
### 2. 15-Minute Weekly Sync (no long meetings)
Hold a 15-minute check-in Sunday after dinner, with only 3 questions for each person (including the older child, if age-appropriate):
1. What do you need for the week?
2. What can you take on?
3. Are there any fixed appointments/commitments others need to know about?
No agenda, no notes unless there is a critical item (e.g., baby’s vaccine appointment, mom’s 2-week postpartum check). No follow-up check-ins during the week unless there is an urgent need.
### 3. Role-Based Weekly Zones (no task lists)
Skip endless to-do lists by assigning each parent a core zone for the week, with no need to negotiate individual tasks:
- One parent owns the *Newborn + Mom Care Zone*: handles all baby care (except scheduled shifts), mom’s meds, and care team check-ins
- The other parent owns the *Older Kid + Household Zone*: handles dropoff/pickup, meals, chores, and errands
Rotate zones weekly to avoid burnout. Swaps are only for urgent needs, no haggling over small tasks.
### 4. 3-Point Care Handoff (no logs)
When switching caregiver shifts, share only 3 quick updates to avoid miscommunication and eliminate the need for written logs:
1. Last baby care milestone (last feed, last diaper change, any fussiness/concerns)
2. Mom’s last meds/any immediate needs
3. Older child’s urgent updates (forgot their lunch, has a last-minute playdate)
### 5. Mom’s No-Ask Request System
Post a 1-page list on the fridge with pre-written, common requests (e.g., "I need: water, pain meds, a snack, help holding the baby, someone to pick up [older child], 30 mins of quiet time"). Mom just points to the list instead of having to coordinate asks, eliminating admin for her during recovery.
### 6. Older Child’s Static Whiteboard
Put a $1 whiteboard in the kitchen with 3 fixed sections (no updates needed unless the weekly sync changes plans):
1. This Week’s Schedule (school, activities, who’s picking them up)
2. My Weekly Chores (age-appropriate, pre-assigned at the weekly sync)
3. Ask an Adult (for things they need help with)
This gives the older child autonomy, eliminates repeated "what’s for dinner?" / "who’s picking me up?" questions, and requires zero digital tracking.
---
## Minimal-Tool Coordination Systems (<5 mins of setup, no ongoing admin)
Only use these if needed, and stick to tools the family already uses:
### 1. Shared Group Chat (use existing iMessage/WhatsApp)
Set strict rules to avoid clutter:
- Only 3 types of messages allowed: urgent needs, appointment updates, weekly sync reminders
- Pin critical appointments (mom’s checkups, baby’s vaccines, older kid’s events) to the top of the chat so no one has to dig for them
- Use built-in chat reminders for meds, appointments, so no separate calendar is needed if you don’t already use one.
### 2. Shared Calendar (only if you already use one, e.g., Google Calendar, iCloud Calendar)
Only add events that require other people’s presence: no personal events, no grocery runs, no date nights unless the other parent needs to cover care. No extra data entry needed—just add events as they come up.
### 3. Minimal Critical Task Tracking (only if required by care teams)
Use your phone’s built-in reminder app for recurring tasks (mom’s pain meds, baby’s vitamin D drops, older child’s allergy meds). If a care provider requires a log of doses/symptoms, use your phone’s built-in notes app to jot down times as you go—no fancy health tracking apps needed. *No need to track baby sleep, mom’s mood, or older kid’s screen time unless there is a specific clinical or pre-existing family rule concern.*
### 4. Outside Helper Coordination (for meals, drop-in help)
Skip meal train apps that require you to share your address, dietary restrictions, and contact info. Instead:
- Use a free, no-sign-up shared Google Sheet with only 3 columns: Name, What they’re bringing/doing, Time. No extra columns for personal info.
- Or pin a note in your group chat where helpers can add what they’re bringing.
- Add a single line of instructions: "Leave items on the porch, no need to come in" to avoid extra coordination.
---
## Explicitly Avoid (to cut unnecessary overhead)
- Baby tracking apps that require logging every feed, diaper, or sleep: these are huge time sinks, and almost never required by pediatricians unless there is a specific feeding/health concern.
- Family task management apps (e.g., Cozi, Todoist) that require everyone to sign up and log tasks: these create more work than they solve for tired parents and kids who don’t want to use an app.
- Spreadsheets with 10+ columns for tracking every part of care: only use a shared sheet for outside helpers, and keep it to 3 columns max.
- Unrequested symptom or milestone logs for mom, baby, or older child: only track what your care team explicitly asks for.
### Optional Low-Effort Add-On
Assign one parent as the single point of contact for all medical providers (pediatrician, OB, lactation consultant, etc.). They relay updates to the rest of the family and collect instructions from care teams, so no one has to repeat information to multiple providers or sit on redundant calls.
